title: Embouchure and transposing on clarinet
summary: He used his lips over his teeth; B-flat and A clarinet; transposing with McCurdy and violin retuning.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: When you played the clarinet, even when you had your own teeth, did you bite onto the mouthpiece with your teeth,
or use your lips? No, no, I used my lips. Yeah.
Covered the upper teeth with your lips. Yeah, yeah. Did anybody teach you to do that, this fellow there? No, no. That's what I said.
I just picked it up and just, you know.
Professor Minetta says that Sam Dutre taught him to do that. Oh, yeah. Oh, he was, he was, he was. Do you remember George Barquet, did he, did he bit? Well, I don't remember. You don't remember.
I don't remember what, I, I.
Or Teo, do you remember how he did that?

No, I don't, I don't remember how he did it. But I, I tried to figure out, you know, I had a B in the A clarinet. See, we used to get in and use it too, you know. Yes. Well, I couldn't, I couldn't transpose like, probably used to play with the Robichaud, what is his name again? McCurdy? McCurdy, yeah. He could transpose, you know. He could play an A on his B. But now, for me to play that A music, I'd make C. And the violin player had to tune over again, you know, make A and I'd make C. Then I could play that A part, my part, see. So Robichaud, he, I told him that so he couldn't figure it out, you know. But just like he couldn't figure that out, I couldn't figure out a transpose. You see? I used my own ideas about that.
